basis: The printing heads this quaestio 'VERS. 18.' and it opens '(Vers. 18.) Et Melchisedech rex Salem protulit panem et vinum, et ipse Sacerdos Dei'. The printing's caput and the lemma's own words, matched against the Clementine, name the same chapter.
date_basis: Written at Bethlehem and named in Jerome's own De viris illustribus 135, finished in 393, among the works already published; the preface announces it as the first of a series of Hebrew Questions on the whole of Scripture that he never continued. The early 390s is as close as the evidence held here reaches. The date is the writing, not the 1845 printing and not Vallarsi's 1767 edition.
text: (Vers. 18.) Et Melchisedech rex Salem protulit panem et vinum, et ipse Sacerdos Dei excelsi, et benedixit ei. Quia semel opusculum nostrum, vel Quaestionum Hebraicarum, vel Traditionum congregatio est, propterea quid Hebraei de hoc sentiant, inferamus. Aiunt hunc esse Sem filium Noe: et supputantes annos vitae ipsius, ostendunt eum ad Isaac usque vixisse, omnesque primogenitos Noe donec sacerdotio fungeretur Aaron, fuisse pontifices. Porro Salem, rex Jerusalem dicitur, quae prius Salem appellabatur. Melchisedech autem beatus Apostolus ad Hebraeos (VII, 3), sine patre et matre commemorans, ad Christum refert, et per Christum ad gentium Ecclesiam. Omnis enim capitis gloria refertur ad membra, eo quod praeputium habens, Abrahae benedixerit circumciso, et in Abraham Levi, et per Levi Aaron: de quo postea sacerdotium. Ex quo colligi vult, sacerdotium Ecclesiae habentis praeputium, benedixisse circumciso sacerdotio Synagogae. Quod autem ait: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedech (Ps. CIX, 4): mysterium nostrum in verbo ordinis significatur: nequaquam per Aaron irrationalibus victimis immolandis, sed oblato pane et vino: id est, corpore et sanguine Domini Jesu.
